wsj.summary_analysis: Lilly's third-quarter 2017 report, published October 24, centered on the announcement that the company was exploring a spinoff or sale of its Elanco animal-health business, a unit that had contributed 15% of Lilly's revenue the prior year but faced rising competition. Elanco generated $740.6 million in third-quarter revenue, up 5% year over year, against total company revenue of $5.66 billion, up 9%, driven mainly by newer pharmaceutical products including Trulicity and Basaglar. The article cites J.P. Morgan estimates that a sale of Elanco could fetch $14 billion to $16 billion, assuming a valuation multiple comparable to market leader Zoetis. CEO Dave Ricks said in an interview that investors have repeatedly questioned whether Elanco makes sense inside the company, and that Lilly decided to review its options now because it has largely finished integrating past acquisitions, notably the $5 billion 2015 purchase of Novartis's animal-health business; he said the human-drug business, which had leaned on Elanco during a period of patent expirations, is now on better footing, and he expected to decide on a course of action by mid-2018, with an IPO, merger, sale, or retaining the unit all on the table. Within Elanco, livestock revenue fell 6% on competitive pressure in the U.S. cattle industry, while companion-animal revenue rose 35%, mainly from the Boehringer Ingelheim feline, canine and rabies vaccine acquisition, though increased competition and lower realized prices hurt that business too. GAAP EPS fell to 53 cents from 73 cents a year earlier, while adjusted EPS rose to $1.05 from 88 cents; the company cut its GAAP EPS guidance for the year to $1.73-$1.83 from $2.51-$2.61 due to restructuring charges, while raising adjusted EPS guidance to $4.15-$4.25 from $4.10-$4.20.

The decline appears tied less to the reported numbers than to the uncertainty introduced by the strategic-review announcement itself: as detailed above, Lilly had for years dismissed spinoff speculation, and formally putting a $14-16 billion asset that generates 15% of company revenue into play, without committing to a specific outcome and with a decision not expected until mid-2018, creates a period of ambiguity that can weigh on shares even alongside otherwise solid quarterly performance. The article also notes competitive pressure within Elanco's livestock segment, down 6%, and lower realized prices in its companion-animal business, both of which complicate the bull case for what the unit could ultimately fetch in any transaction.

wsj.summary_analysis: Lilly's second-quarter 2018 report, published July 24, confirmed the company would take public a minority stake, under 20%, in its Elanco animal-health business as a first step toward eventually shedding the unit, following the October 2017 announcement that it was reviewing strategic options including a sale. CFO Josh Smiley said in an interview that an IPO was chosen over a straight sale because it was more tax-efficient, and that Lilly wanted to capitalize on strong investor appetite for animal-health companies, adding that investors appreciate the underlying growth of the sector. The article draws a direct historical parallel to Pfizer's 2013 IPO of a minority stake in its Zoetis animal-health business, followed by a full spinoff to shareholders, a path Lilly could also eventually take, and notes Zoetis, now the largest animal-health company, carries a roughly $40 billion market cap and a price-to-earnings ratio more than double Pfizer's, trading near all-time highs. Elanco recorded about $3.1 billion in sales last year, 13% of total Lilly revenue, with J.P. Morgan previously estimating it could fetch $14-16 billion in a sale; Smiley said the animal-health market is expected to grow about 5% annually, benefiting from less pricing pressure and generic competition and shorter development cycles than human pharmaceuticals. On the underlying quarter, Elanco revenue grew just 0.9% to $792.1 million, while total company revenue rose 9.1% to $6.36 billion, boosted by higher sales of Humalog, Trulicity and Basaglar. GAAP results showed a $259.9 million loss, or 25 cents a share, versus a $1 billion profit a year earlier, but adjusted EPS of $1.50 beat the average analyst estimate of $1.30 on Thomson Reuters, with the GAAP loss tied to charges related to two acquisitions.
wsj.why_moved: Shares rose 2.9% to $91.49 in early afternoon trading the day of the report, and the article's numbers explain why directly: adjusted EPS of $1.50 beat the $1.30 analysts had modeled by a wide margin, and total revenue growth of 9.1% was driven by the core human-pharmaceutical products, Humalog, Trulicity and Basaglar, rather than by the smaller, slower-growing Elanco unit. The confirmation of the Elanco IPO plan discussed above likely reinforced the positive reaction by giving investors a concrete timeline and structure, a sub-20% stake, filing expected within weeks, process complete in the second half of the year, after nine months of uncertainty since the October 2017 review was first announced. The Zoetis comparison cited in the article, a business trading near all-time highs at a rich multiple, offers a benchmark for what a public Elanco could be valued at, which may have added to enthusiasm beyond the quarter's core results alone.
